slides.text: This project builds a coding agent for PLC Structured Text. The goal is to generate a real function block, compile it with CODESYS, repair compiler errors, and check its behavior across scans. I implemented a small Python harness and compared it with an established tool-using agent. The comparison uses thirty two tasks, two agent frameworks, and two model routes from the available relay service. Every reported result has saved evidence.

The dataset includes all twenty official questions and twelve independently constructed questions. Each task has a typed interface, initial state, priorities, temporal specifications, and fixed tests. Together they contain two hundred and seven LTL properties and eighty one test cases. Inputs are sampled before an invocation, and outputs are observed after that same invocation. For the guarded motor, a stop request must clear the run output in the current scan. This explicit convention avoids confusing pre-scan state with end-of-scan output.

The harness first extracts the interface and behavioral constraints. It then asks the model for structured source, inserts that source into an isolated CODESYS project, and compiles it. If the compiler reports errors, the harness sends the current code and focused diagnostics back for repair. There are at most two repairs after the initial attempt. Every candidate and response is retained. Compilation success ends generation, while functional testing remains a separate stage. This control loop makes the system more than a single prompt.

Compilation is performed by the installed CODESYS Development System. The backend was checked with a valid program, an intentionally invalid program, and a corrected program. Their actual error counts were zero, two, and zero. All three processes returned exit code zero, so the wrapper cannot trust the exit code alone. It rebuilds the application and checks diagnostic severities, the submitted source hash, a unique request identifier, and evidence that the function block was compiled. This slide shows an actual diagnostic excerpt.

The baseline is the unmodified smolagents Tool Calling Agent. Its normal agent loop selects the shared compiler tool. Our harness controls generation and repair explicitly. Both use the same DeepSeek route and Kimi route, the same tasks, the same three-build limit, and the same request settings. Codex was initially preferred, but its local tool policy prevented the required execution, so the baseline was changed before the full campaign. The baseline can make an extra model request to produce its final answer. That difference is disclosed.

All one hundred and twenty eight generation runs were executed. Final compilation rates were ninety point six percent, eighty four point four percent, eighty one point three percent, and ninety six point nine percent for E one through E four. These rates keep infrastructure failures in the denominator. The runtime column counts passed cases among actually evaluated cases. Each condition plans eighty one cases, so coverage must also be considered. Actual simulation found behavioral failures in some compiling candidates. These single-run results do not establish a general framework ranking.

Here is a repair performed by our own harness on the bounded fault-retry task. The first candidate used an enum literal named LOCKED and a Boolean output named Locked. CODESYS treated those names case-insensitively and reported three type errors. The model received those diagnostics and prefixed the enum literals, preserving the required output name. The next actual build had zero errors after one repair. Separate source hashes and logs verify the change. Runtime correctness is checked independently, rather than inferred from this build result.

The project establishes a working generation, compilation, and repair loop, plus a reproducible comparison with actual compiler and runtime evidence. Its limits remain clear. Functional evaluation covers finite scalar traces, while physical timing and composite caller bindings need further work. The LTL specifications are not complete formal proofs. There is one run per task and condition, and the relay does not independently establish model identity or pricing. The next steps are broader runtime adapters and repeated experiments.
